topic: The Pi Collision Mystery: How Colliding Blocks Calculate the Universe's Most Famous Constant
target_audience: Undergraduate Physics/Math students or Advanced High School Students

sections.title: The Hook: The Counting Machine
sections.content: Introduce a thought experiment: Two sliding blocks and a wall on a frictionless surface. We count every time the blocks hit each other or the wall. If the blocks have specific mass ratios, the total number of collisions magically yields the digits of Pi.
sections.example: Visualizing a 'Collision Counter' scoreboard above a small block (1kg) and a massive block (100kg). As the massive block pushes the small one against the wall, the counter ends exactly at 31.

sections.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Conservation Laws
sections.content: Briefly review Elastic Collisions. Explain that kinetic energy (1/2 mv²) and momentum (mv) are conserved. This defines the physical constraints of our 'system's state'.
sections.example: A 'Venn Diagram' of energy and momentum: Energy conservation creates an ellipse on a velocity graph (v1 vs v2), while momentum conservation dictates the jump between states during a collision.

sections.title: Geometric Transformation: From Ellipse to Circle
sections.content: Introduce a coordinate shift. By scaling the velocity of the larger block (V) by the square root of its mass ratio (√M/m), the elliptical energy equation transforms into a perfect circle: x² + y² = C. This is the 'State Space'.
sections.example: An animation showing a squashed oval being stretched vertically until it becomes a perfect circle. The position of a point on this circle represents the current velocities of both blocks.

sections.title: The Physics of a Bounce: A Reflection in State Space
sections.content: Explain that each collision (block-to-block or block-to-wall) corresponds to a reflection of a point across a line in this circular state space. The 'angle' of these reflections is determined by the mass ratio.
sections.example: A laser beam bouncing inside a circular mirror. Each 'ping' of the laser against the side represents one physical collision in the real world.

sections.title: Connecting to Pi: The Arc Length
sections.content: Show that for a mass ratio of 100^n, the small angle of each bounce is approximately 1/10^n radians. To travel the full 'arc' of the circle and reverse the massive block's direction, the number of bounces required is Pi divided by that small angle.
sections.example: Using a mass ratio of 1:10,000 (100^2). The animation shows the 'laser' making tiny steps around the circle. After 314 hits, the large block finally moves away, mirroring the digits 3.14.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Power of Phase Space
sections.content: Summarize how abstract mathematical spaces (Phase Space) reveal hidden constants in physical systems. Pi isn't just about circles in geometry; it's about the symmetry of energy conservation.
sections.example: A final side-by-side view: A 'Mega-Block' (mass 1,000,000kg) creating 3,141 collisions, while a digital clock overlays the digits of Pi simultaneously.
